edits.find: The question isn't "what's abnormal?" — it's "what drives this outcome?" Uncontrolled hypertension is the direct mechanical driver of decompensation: ↑ afterload → ↑ LV wall stress → remodeling → pump failure → admission. Lipids matter for ischemic events over years; BP matters for decompensations over months. Time horizon is the whole question.
edits.with: Target the factor that drives this outcome, not simply the value that is abnormal. Uncontrolled hypertension is the direct mechanical driver of decompensation. It raises afterload, which raises LV (left ventricular) wall stress and leads to remodeling, pump failure and admission. Lipids matter for ischemic events over years. BP (blood pressure) matters for decompensations over months.

edits.find: Why HDL is bait Low HDL predicts risk but raising it pharmacologically has never reduced events. Niacin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) — no benefit on top of statin, plus harm. CETP inhibitors raised HDL up to 130% with no benefit; torcetrapib increased mortality. Fibrates (FIELD, ACCORD-Lipid) — no consistent mortality benefit. HDL is a risk marker, not a drug target. And when the stem says "prevent cardiovascular mortality," only statins have reproducible mortality data (4S, HPS, JUPITER).
edits.with: HDL as a drug target Low HDL (high-density lipoprotein) predicts risk, but raising it with drugs has never reduced events. Niacin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) gave no benefit on top of a statin and added harm. CETP inhibitors (cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitors) raised HDL up to 130% with no benefit, and torcetrapib increased mortality. Fibrates (FIELD, ACCORD-Lipid) showed no consistent mortality benefit. HDL is a risk marker, not a drug target. For preventing cardiovascular mortality, only statins have reproducible mortality data (4S, HPS, JUPITER).

edits.find:
Guideline currency — the terminology was retired The 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline discourages "typical / atypical / nonanginal." The problem: "atypical" was meant to signal angina without classic features, but clinicians were reading it as "not cardiac" — the opposite of its purpose. The preferred descriptors are now cardiac · possible cardiac · noncardiac:
  • Cardiac — central, retrosternal, squeezing, pressure, exertional
  • Possible cardiac — stabbing, tearing, ripping, burning ← where epigastric burning lands
  • Noncardiac — pleuritic, positional, fleeting
Question banks still key "atypical angina" for a 2-of-3 presentation, so know both vocabularies: score the three criteria for the exam, describe by probability in clinic. Note the shift does not change management — "possible cardiac" still gets risk-stratified and tested.

edits.find: Mechanism chains they test link by link Aldosterone → ENaC upregulation in the collecting duct → Na⁺ reabsorption → electronegative lumen → K⁺ and H⁺ secretion → hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis. Aldosterone escape (ANP + pressure natriuresis) means sodium plateaus and there is no edema — a normal sodium does not argue against the diagnosis. For renovascular disease, read the verb: "initiated by" → renin; "directly mediates vasoconstriction" → angiotensin II; "causes the hypokalemia" → aldosterone.
edits.with: Mechanism chains Aldosterone upregulates ENaC (epithelial sodium channel) in the collecting duct, which increases Na⁺ reabsorption. The lumen becomes electronegative, which drives K⁺ and H⁺ secretion. The result is hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Aldosterone escape, through ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) and pressure natriuresis, means sodium plateaus and there is no edema. A normal sodium does not argue against the diagnosis. In renovascular disease, renin initiates the cascade, angiotensin II directly mediates vasoconstriction, and aldosterone causes the hypokalemia.
edits.note: voice: .pearls; rhetorical label reworded, arrow chain split, question framing removed
reworded_label: Mechanism chains they test link by link
